title: Mirror-Symmetric Chain
statement:
You get the head of a singly linked list of digits. Return true if the values read the same from the front to the back as from the back to the front, otherwise false.

Try to do it in O(n) time with only O(1) extra memory. (Changing the list temporarily is allowed; good practice is to put it back.)

examples.why: Front to back and back to front both read 4, 7, 7, 4.
The same digits with the same counts, but backwards it reads 7, 4, 7, 4.
With an odd length the middle node is only compared with itself.

hints: With an array you would compare position i with position n − 1 − i. A singly linked list cannot walk backwards. What is the simplest way around that?
To avoid extra memory, find the middle of the list. A slow pointer moving one step and a fast pointer moving two steps does it in one pass.
Reverse the second half in place, walk the first half and the reversed second half together comparing values, then reverse the second half again to restore the list.

explain.intuition:
A palindrome check compares the first value with the last, the second with the second-to-last, and so on. A singly linked list only goes forward. The easy fix is to copy the values into an array, at the cost of O(n) memory.

To stay in O(1) memory, make the second half go backwards. Find the middle with slow and fast pointers (when fast reaches the end, slow is halfway). Reverse the links of the second half; now you can walk inward from both ends at the same time. Reversing that half once more afterwards leaves the caller's list exactly as it was.
steps: Move slow one step and fast two steps while fast.next and fast.next.next exist. slow ends on the last node of the first half.
Reverse the list that starts at slow.next; call its new head second.
Walk p = head and q = second together while q exists, and record a mismatch if p.val !== q.val.
Reverse second again and attach it back to slow.next.
Return whether there was no mismatch.
pitfalls: Comparing sorted values or digit counts. [4, 7, 4, 7] has matching counts but is not symmetric.
Getting the middle wrong for odd lengths. With the stopping rule above, the middle node stays in the first half and is never compared, which is correct.
Leaving the list reversed. The answer is right, but the caller's data is now broken, which is a classic side-effect bug.

solutions.title: Copy values into an array
solutions.idea: Read every value into an array, then compare from both ends with two indexes.

solutions.title: Reverse the second half, compare, restore
solutions.idea: Find the middle with slow and fast pointers, reverse the second half in place, compare it with the first half, then reverse it back.

followups: Solve it with recursion that compares on the way back up. What does it cost in memory, and why can it crash on 100 000 nodes?
The list is shared with other threads that may read it while you work. Is the in-place approach still acceptable?
